# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) have markedly improved the outcomes of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), but their enduring presence in the vessel wall has been linked to persistent inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, impaired vasomotion, and a continuing risk of very late stent failure [1]. In patients who receive metallic drug-eluting coronary stents, adverse events such as late target-lesion failure may be related in part to the persistent presence of the metallic stent frame in the coronary-vessel wall, and bioresorbable vascular scaffolds have been developed to attempt to improve long-term outcomes [2]. The concept of "vascular restoration therapy" envisages a device that provides transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery, followed by complete resorption with recovery of physiological vascular function [3].

## Early clinical experience

The first-in-man Absorb device, an everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactic acid scaffold, was tested in the ABSORB Cohort A study of 30 patients with single de novo lesions [3,4]. The Cohort A trial enrolled 30 patients with a single de novo native coronary artery lesion; at four years the hierarchical ID-MACE remained 3.4%, demonstrating a sustained low event rate without late complications such as stent thrombosis [3]. Serial multimodality imaging suggested restoration of vasomotion, late lumen gain, and plaque regression as the scaffold resorbed [5].

## Pivotal randomized trials

These promising signals prompted larger randomized comparisons against the cobalt–chromium everolimus-eluting Xience stent. In ABSORB II, despite rapid dissemination of an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold for the treatment of coronary artery disease, no data from comparisons with its metallic stent counterpart had been available [6]. ABSORB II was complemented by ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan, which used angiographic endpoints [7,8]. The pivotal regulatory trial was ABSORB III, which randomized 2008 patients. In this large, multicenter trial, 2008 patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold or an everolimus-eluting cobalt–chromium stent, with the primary endpoint of target-lesion failure—cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-lesion revascularization—at 1 year [9]. A patient-level pooled meta-analysis of four trials confirmed comparable 1-year efficacy [10].

## Emergence of safety concerns

Longer follow-up tempered initial enthusiasm. ABSORB III demonstrated noninferior target lesion failure at 1 year, but between 1 and 3 years and cumulative to 3 years, adverse event rates—particularly target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis—were increased after the scaffold [11]. A landmark meta-analysis crystallized the concern. Among 2309 patients with the bioresorbable scaffold, the rate of definite or probable stent thrombosis was 1.3% compared with 0.5% in the 1382 patients who received a Xience stent [12]. The investigator-initiated AIDA all-comers trial reinforced this. In a preliminary report there was no significant difference in the primary outcome of target-vessel failure, but treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years [13]. Final 5-year AIDA results and 3-year ABSORB III data extended these observations [14,15].

Multiple meta-analyses converged on this signal. A weighted meta-analysis of seven randomized trials showed a higher rate of target lesion failure and an almost threefold higher rate of device thrombosis with the scaffold compared with Xience, extending beyond the first year [16]. Individual-patient-data analyses similarly found excess risk [17,18], and three-year pooled data confirmed inferiority. At 3 years, the scaffold was associated with higher rates of target lesion failure and definite/probable scaffold thrombosis compared with DES [19].

## The role of technique and resorption timing

Two findings reframed interpretation of these data. First, the excess risk appeared confined to the resorption period. The period of excess risk for the first-generation Absorb scaffold ended at 3 years, when poly-L-lactic acid bioresorption is complete; thereafter event rates were comparable or lower with the scaffold [20]. Time-varying pooled analyses supported this temporal pattern [21,22]. Second, implantation technique mattered. Procedural technique may affect clinical outcomes after scaffold implantation, and prior studies suggesting such a relationship had not adjusted for baseline characteristics influencing operator choice [23]. Suboptimal vessel sizing and lack of aggressive lesion preparation, together with thick struts, predisposed to thrombosis [24,25]. The ABSORB IV trial incorporated improved technique and angina-focused endpoints [26], and the COMPARE-ABSORB trial enrolled higher-risk patients [27]. These data led the manufacturer to withdraw Absorb from commercial sale and underpinned recommendations for prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy [28].

## Next-generation scaffolds

Attention has shifted to thinner-strut and metallic-alloy platforms. The sirolimus-eluting magnesium scaffold (Magmaris) was studied in BIOSOLVE-II. The second-generation drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold was assessed in patients with de novo coronary artery lesions in this prospective, multicentre, first-in-man trial [29]. The third-generation DREAMS 3G magnesium scaffold has shown encouraging early results. BIOMAG-I, the first trial of the new-generation sirolimus-eluting magnesium scaffold DREAMS 3G, showed low angiographic in-scaffold late lumen loss and excellent clinical safety and efficacy at 1 year, the end of the device resorption period [30].

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable scaffolds embody an attractive physiological concept, but first-generation devices were limited by excess mid-term thrombosis tied to thick struts, resorption-phase fragility, and operator technique. Thinner-strut polymeric and magnesium-based platforms, optimized implantation, and prolonged antiplatelet therapy may yet allow the promise of transient vascular support to be realized; robust long-term randomized data remain essential.
